content: The addition of micronutrient powders (MNPs) to simulated real-world diets was shown to reduce or eliminate nutrient gaps for several key nutrients, including iron, B vitamins, and zinc. The evidence supporting reductions in iron deficiency was of high certainty, while evidence for anemia, serum ferritin concentrations, and weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ) was of moderate certainty. However, evidence for hemoglobin (Hgb) concentrations was of low certainty. A systematic review of fortified cereal grain-based complementary foods identified 16 trials, including eight individually randomized controlled trials (RCTs), seven cluster-randomized RCTs, and one non-randomized controlled trial. Most of these studies were conducted in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) with sample sizes ranging from 40 to 1,465 children aged 6–60 months. The duration of the studies varied, with three being short-term (three feeding sessions to three consecutive days), most being longer-term (10 weeks to 18 months), and one having variable duration. The interventions included fortified wheat-based products, maize/corn-based products, rice or rice cereal, pearl millet, and legume or cereal-legume blends. The number of studies for each fortified food ranged from one to five, and the number of fortificants varied widely. For example, six studies included only iron as a fortificant, while three studies included 10 or more micronutrients. This variability made it impossible to isolate the effects of different micronutrient formulations on outcomes. For anemia and Hgb concentrations, the certainty of evidence was moderate, while it was low for serum ferritin concentrations. No effects were observed on zinc deficiency, vitamin A deficiency, or growth outcomes. Additionally, no impact was found on fine and gross motor scores. Developmental outcomes were rated as moderate to low certainty. One trial involving 97 children reported no differences in diarrhea episodes, fever, or acute respiratory infections. Dietary modeling showed that the daily inclusion of Super Cereal Plus (SCP) in a feasible best-case diet introduced gaps in potassium, zinc, thiamine, and choline. Simulated real-world diets from three LMICs (Bangladesh, Malawi, and Mexico) were compared to alternative patterns with daily SCP inclusion. In Bangladesh and Malawi, where diets were dominated by staple foods, SCP increased the percentage of children meeting the nutrient reference values (NRVs) for B vitamins and minerals, except potassium. However, deficits remained for five to seven key nutrients, including significant deficits in iron. In Mexico, where diets were more diverse, SCP increased intakes of iron and zinc but decreased intakes of other nutrients, particularly potassium, due to food displacement. Deficits in two to five key nutrients, including large deficits in iron, persisted. Consumption of fortified cereal grain-based complementary foods by children aged 6–23 months improved indicators of iron status but not zinc, vitamin A, or growth outcomes. Children consuming fortified cereal-based complementary foods had better mental skill development scores and motor development scores but no improvements in fine and gross motor scores when assessed separately. Dietary modeling found that SCP improved some nutrient intakes but left deficits, especially in iron. A systematic review on fortified versus unfortified milk for children aged 12–23 months identified eight studies involving 2,905 children, mostly RCTs. Evidence was of low certainty overall, except for Hgb concentrations, which were rated as moderate certainty. Children consuming fortified milk were less likely to be anemic or have iron-deficiency anemia (IDA) but showed no difference in iron deficiency (serum ferritin concentrations <12 µg). No differences were observed in weight, stunting, or wasting. However, children consuming unfortified milk had lower weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ), weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ), height velocity, and weight velocity. Fortified milk had no effect on oral health or respiratory infections but was associated with fewer episodes of diarrhea. Small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) were evaluated in LMICs for their effects on mortality, growth, development, anemia, and micronutrient status. Inclusion criteria for the reviews required prospective RCTs conducted in LMICs with children aged 6–24 months receiving at least three months of supplementation. Six trials reported no effect on diarrheal or malarial morbidity, while two trials in Bangladesh showed reduced prevalence and duration of diarrhea, pneumonia, and dysentery favoring the intervention. Supplemented children had greater length-for-age z-scores (LAZ), WAZ, head circumference-for-age z-scores, and less severe stunting, wasting, and acute malnutrition. No differences were observed in executive function or child overweight/high BMI. Follow-up studies in Ghana and Bangladesh found no greater preference for or consumption of sweet or high-fat foods in the intervention group. Dietary modeling showed that daily SQ-LNS supplementation reduced but did not eliminate iron gaps for infants aged 6–8 months. However, it introduced gaps in potassium and choline due to food displacement. For 9–11-month-olds, daily SQ-LNS supplementation reduced the iron gap. In simulated real-world patterns in Bangladesh, Malawi, and Mexico, daily SQ-LNS supplementation eliminated gaps for B vitamins (except for 1-year-olds in Bangladesh) and zinc and reduced or eliminated calcium gaps. Potassium gaps were reduced for most groups. Iron gaps were reduced in infancy and eliminated or nearly eliminated for 1-year-olds. However, gaps in iron, choline, and potassium remained for most age groups. Evidence from RCTs shows that children consuming SQ-LNS had reduced mortality, were less likely to be stunted, wasted, underweight, or severely undernourished, and had higher developmental scores. SQ-LNS also reduced anemia, iron deficiency (ID), and IDA. Indicators of vitamin A status were higher among supplemented children compared to controls. No differences were observed in diarrheal or malarial morbidity, nor were there long-term preferences for unhealthy foods or beverages. Dietary modeling found that daily SQ-LNS supplementation reduced but did not eliminate iron gaps for infants aged 6–8 months and introduced gaps in potassium and choline. The balance of benefits and harms for MNPs, fortified cereal grain-based complementary foods, fortified milks, and SQ-LNS likely favors their consumption, although there is uncertainty for MNPs and fortified milks. The benefits were deemed moderate, with variability depending on the product, and harms were judged to be negligible or uncertain. Caregivers reported that children preferred the taste of fortified products, but their own preferences depended on taste, aroma, color, content, and ease of preparation. Changes in these characteristics led to dislike and discontinuation of use. The certainty of evidence for values and preferences was low to very low, indicating variability in caregiver willingness to use fortified products. Resource implications for these products are relevant to budgets of international organizations and national governments. Distribution depends on supply chains and logistics, with costs including production, packaging, transport, and distribution. Opportunity costs of implementing these interventions instead of others must also be considered. The resource implications for MNPs, fortified cereal grain-based complementary foods, fortified milks, and SQ-LNS were deemed moderate and context-dependent. Responsive feeding, defined as feeding practices that encourage autonomous eating in response to physiological and developmental needs, is increasingly recognized as an important component of infant and young child feeding. It involves reciprocity between the child and caregiver during feeding, with the caregiver recognizing and responding to the child’s hunger and satiety cues.
